question: And then my second question is just around iCloud+. It seems like it's becoming a more strategic product just given the tie-in with home security as well as the potential monetization opportunity for Apple Intelligence. So I was just wondering, what are you seeing on iCloud+? Are there any tailwinds in terms of attach rates, just particularly given the rising cost for increased storage options on iPhone and the company's push into home products?

This is something we're very excited about. We have these iCloud+ plans that now include Apple TV and Apple Arcade in more than 100 countries and regions where we think we can really reach new potential subscribers. And then as you mentioned, we think there's good opportunities on Apple Intelligence. There's going to be some usage limits on features that rely on server side models, which include Siri AI and intelligent photo editing and some other things like that. And so anyone who needs greater capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future. So kind of to your point, in the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we've been adding more capabilities and features to it. Operator, could we get the next question, please.

question: John, congrats on your first quarter here. So as the world of AI evolves from chatbots to consumer agents, it seems like there are growing opportunities for Apple. It also seems like there are risks. And John, I'd just love to get your perspective on what role you want Apple and Siri AI to play in kind of this consumer-agentic AI landscape? And just how you look at any potential risks of some of these agents trying to encroach on your services business? And then a quick follow-up, please.
answer: Look, we -- first and foremost, we are incredibly excited to launch Siri AI alongside the latest generation of Apple Intelligence features. Siri has long been popular with our users with more than 2.5 billion requests every day. And with Siri AI, we really have the kind of the Siri that we always wanted. It's primarily request-based today. But as we talked about at WWDC, it's built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time. As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. So we're pushing really hard on that with Siri AI, but we're also really encouraged the fact that Apple devices, we think, are the best places to use all forms of AI.
asks: [answered*] Apple/Siri AI’s role in the consumer-agentic AI landscape | [partial] Risks of agents encroaching on Apple’s services business | [not_answered] Quick follow-up
rationale: He addressed Siri’s role and gave a broad safety view, but did not directly answer the services-encroachment risk.

question: I appreciate that, John. And then just quickly as a follow-up, how should we -- if we take a big step back, how should we think about the durability of services growth? Just I realize that was 10% in the September quarter. We're a little bit below that in the December quarter. As certain things like search evolves and regulatory changes impact App Store monetization, are there new services that we should be looking towards that you believe can become a more sizable offset to maybe take some pressure off these historically important revenue streams?
answer: Thanks for the question. Let me take this one. Let me start by just talking through kind of what we did -- we talked about during the December quarter. Services grew by 10% year-over-year. And we look at that relative to the June quarter, foreign exchange was the main driver in that change on year-on-year growth rate sequentially. We saw -- we continue to see strong performance in September in many of our service categories, all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, including our first-party Apple Ads and September quarter record in music. But I think it's important to kind of step back also and look at the progression of what we've seen in our services business over the last several quarters. I think it's an important backdrop. And so we spoke about on the last call, we expected foreign exchange to be the largest driver of the change in the year-on-year growth rate from the March to September quarter. This ended up being a significant headwind of about 4 percentage points, and we expect additional sequential headwind of about another 0.5 percentage point for the services business as we go into the December quarter. We've also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store. And during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store. At the same time, we did see some headwinds …
asks: [answered*] How to think about the durability of services growth | [answered] Whether new services can offset pressure from search/App Store monetization
rationale: Management gave a substantive long-term services thesis, citing installed-base growth, record usage, and new opportunities like intelligence and Apple Pay.

question: Congrats on mine as well, John, on your first earnings call here. John, you sort of described the iPhone as an intelligent personal hub in your opening comments. And as personal AI agents become more prominent, do you see the potential for the primary customer relationship to shift from the device to the agent over time? And really, given Apple's integration of silicon, hardware and software, where do you see the greatest opportunity to combine things like personal context and on-screen awareness into an agent that can perhaps move beyond answering questions? And how far along do you think Siri is in bringing those pieces together right now?
answer: Thank you, Amit, for the question. Like as I said before, and we said in our announcement, we really do think of the iPhone as the intelligent personal hub. I mean if you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that. And Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to, even Apple doesn't have access to it. And so we think that is a core kind of differentiator that we're excited about. And we're going to continue to push on that. And so I think this is an area that we feel really, really good about.
asks: [not_answered*] Whether the customer relationship could shift from the device to the agent over time | [not_answered] Where Apple sees the biggest opportunity to combine personal context and on-screen awareness into an agent | [not_answered] How far along Siri is in bringing those pieces together today
rationale: Management emphasized iPhone, data access, and privacy, but did not address agent relationship shift, on-screen awareness, or Siri progress.

question: And then, Kevan, the December quarter gross margin, I'm wondering if you could spend a bit of time on that. I think if I exclude all the tariff refunds, you start of implying gross margins will be down about 140 basis points sequentially at least. Can you just separate how much of this is maybe commodity memory inflation versus mix versus -- you called out Siri AI ramp costs as well. Can you just talk about what the different moving parts are as we think about the sequential gross margins, that would be helpful.
answer: Yes, Amit, sounds good. Let me try to address that for you. So as you alluded for the December quarter, we talked about a gross margin outlook of between 45% and 46%. As you said, when you remove the benefit of the tariff refunds in September, the midpoint of the range is a decline sequentially in the magnitude you mentioned. We expect most of that decline to be driven by higher memory costs, and I'll give John kind of the mic here to give you a perspective on that, and then I'll take the balance of your question. Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we've said before, we do believe we'll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. A …
asks: [answered*] December quarter gross margin outlook and sequential change, excluding tariff refunds | [partial] How the sequential gross margin decline breaks down among memory inflation, mix, and Siri AI ramp costs
rationale: They gave the gross margin range and a qualitative driver mix, but not a numeric split across memory, mix, and Siri AI costs.

question: John, my first question, I wanted to ask you about your cash-neutral policy. On one of the previous calls, you guys said that you weren't going to focus on that anymore and that, that was not no longer the policy. What do you -- how -- under your leadership, what do you mean by that? Do you mean like you may go to net debt to buy back stock or do some M&A or go the opposite way and hoard some cash again? Your thoughts on that would be welcome.
answer: Let me take that one. As you know, we did talk about the fact that we were no longer using net cash neutral as a target. I think as we explained on the last call or the last time we talked about that was the fact that we think it makes sense to evaluate our cash and debt position independently and making sure we can optimize that and giving us the right flexibility. We remain committed to our capital allocation philosophy, which is we're going to invest everything we need to put -- invest in our business and return excess cash to shareholders. And so we continue to maintain that discipline. And we do think this removal of net cash neutral gives us flexibility to optimize so we can make the right investments for the company.

question: And then I wanted to ask about services. I realize you only guide one quarter at a time. We talked about the launch of Apple Pay in India, but we continue to see good momentum in emerging markets in our services business, where we had double-digit growth. And so we continue to feel really bullish about all the different elements as we look ahead over the longer arc of time. And I think as John mentioned, we are continuing to improve the features and reach of the existing and new services as well. The example was the expansion of iCloud plans to include Apple TV and Arcade, obviously reaching a lot of new potential subscribers. AppleCare One family is another example of that. question: John, great to have you on the call as CEO. I appreciate the comments on memory. Clearly, you're now competing for memory more so versus historically from pretty well capitalized companies who are signing long-term agreements. So my question is, is Apple changing anything in the way that you are procuring memory? How do you think about the progression of memory over time? And if it continues to be a headwind, is pricing also going to remain dynamic and potentially move higher? And I have a follow-up.
answer: Wamsi, this is Sabih. Let me take that one. So as you know, we have worked with many of our suppliers for decades, and we deeply value their partnership over the years. We know our products would simply not be possible without them, and we look forward to continuing to work together. We're always working hard to improve supply. And as John said earlier, we -- our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from the June to the September quarter. And Wamsi, maybe I'll add here because you asked the question about pricing and how we're managing it. So look, we're trying to manage through this with a number of actions. You heard us talk about the fact we're continuing to pursue lower cost and non-memory components. John mentioned the fact that we have some benefit of carrying inventory. And we did reluctantly make the decision to change pricing in a number of our products, starting with the iPad and Mac in the June time frame and then iPhone more recently in September. I think what we try to do is evaluate in doing all that, we evaluate the unit revenue and margin. And we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations, and we really believe we're balancing this well.
